title: Why is electrification no longer “woke”?
gist: Electrification has shifted from a 'woke' climate mandate to a security and cost imperative, driven by energy shocks (Hormuz closure), AI data-center load and record cooling demand. Grid build-out and permitting reform, not physics, are the binding constraints, and benefits may accrue to fossil incumbents as much as clean energy.

insights.claim: Electrification's political framing has moved from climate and emissions to saving money and energy security, letting it cross the political divide even as US climate rules are rolled back.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Electrification-linked grid names face bipartisan tailwinds framed as resilience and reindustrialization.
insights.locator: The pivot from a green luxury to a national security shield

insights.claim: After the US-Israel attacks on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, fossil fuel importers paid an extra $330 billion for seaborne petroleum products over six months, while recent clean power investments saved importers almost $36 billion in avoided fossil imports.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Quantifies the energy-security case that sustains electrification policy.

insights.claim: The IEA declared an 'Age of Electricity' in February 2026, forecasting annual additions to electricity demand over the next five years 50 percent larger than the average of the previous decade.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Sets a multi-year load-growth baseline for utilities, transmission and equipment makers.

insights.claim: Turkey's COP31 presidency targets raising electricity's share of final energy demand from 21 percent to 35 percent by 2035, and the EU plans to double electricity's share of final consumption to 46 percent by 2040.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Policy targets point to sustained grid and heat-pump/EV demand in Europe.

insights.claim: EVs convert over 77 percent of grid electricity to power at the wheels versus about 12 to 30 percent of gasoline energy for conventional vehicles, and heat pumps are three to four times as efficient as gas boilers.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Efficiency converts directly into cost savings during fuel price shocks.

themes.theme: AI and cooling as load drivers

insights.claim: The IEA estimates global data center electricity consumption will more than double by 2030 to about 945 TWh, slightly more than Japan's total consumption, with AI the main driver.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Anchors power-demand forecasts for AI-exposed utilities and generators.

insights.claim: AI compute needs are growing exponentially while grid capacity grows linearly, so transmission, transformers, substations and long-duration storage are required alongside generation.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Grid equipment and storage are likely bottlenecks.

insights.claim: Electrification can 'free ride' on data-center grid investments: a substation upgrade for a data center also raises local capacity for EV charging and heat pumps, and aggregated storage demand can lower battery costs for other sectors.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Data-center capex has positive spillovers for other electrified loads.

insights.claim: AI's need for firm power has brought geothermal and small modular reactors into the public debate.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Firm-power technologies gain a demand narrative from AI.

insights.claim: Space cooling has accounted for 14 percent of global electricity demand growth since 2015, and in the Middle East and North Africa cooling makes up almost 50 percent of peak demand, forcing grid expansion and distributed storage.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Climate-driven peak load supports grid and storage capex.
insights.locator: Record-breaking heat and increasing cooling needs

insights.claim: The binding constraint on electrification is not physical but the political and regulatory overlay, and permitting reform has become a priority in the US, Canada, Europe, the UK and Australia.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Watch permitting legislation as the gating factor for grid and generation build-out.
insights.locator: A perfect storm for policy reform

insights.claim: Rising electrification does not automatically mean cleaner or more equitable growth; technological shifts pick winners and losers and the tide could lift legacy fossil industries while leaving clean energy behind.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Grid expansion benefits all generation types, including gas, so clean-only exposure is not guaranteed.
insights.quote: rising tide of electrification does not just lift legacy fossil fuel industries
insights.locator: A rising tide lifts all boats? Maybe!
